title: Investigating Gender and Diversity Differences in Hypertension Incidence, Prevalence, Drug Treatment, Efficacy, Adverse Drug Reactions and Health-Related Outcomes: A Large-Scale Retrospective Data Analysis
summary:
High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is one of the most common health conditions worldwide, affecting approximately one in three adults (1). If left untreated or poorly managed, high blood pressure significantly increases the risk of serious health events such as heart attacks and strokes (2). Although effective treatments exist – including lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise, as well as blood pressure-lowering medications – blood pressure is successfully controlled in only about one in four patients (3). Research has shown that factors such as biological sex, gender identity, age, ethnicity, and socioeconomic background can influence how well blood pressure medications work and what side effects they may cause (4). However, these differences are not yet fully understood.
This study aims to investigate whether and how characteristics such as sex, gender, age, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status influence the treatment and control of high blood pressure. Specifically, we want to understand whether certain groups of people respond differently to blood pressure-lowering medications, experience different side effects, or are less likely to have their blood pressure successfully controlled.
To answer these questions, we will analyse existing health data from four large international databases. These databases contain information on a large number of patients, including personal characteristics (such as age, sex, and ethnicity), medical histories, prescribed medications and dosages, blood pressure measurements, laboratory results, and reports of medication side effects (4). By examining this data, we hope to identify patterns that can help improve the treatment of high blood pressure for all people, regardless of their background.
